stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Between 1974 and 1990, folklorist Marit Oyelaran recorded sixty-three versions of a trickster tale told in villages along the Ogun River. The versions disagree about almost everything: the trickster's species, the identity of his victim, even the season in which the story is set. Their endings are strikingly uniform ______ collected decades apart from narrators who had never met, fifty-eight of the versions close with the trickster thanking his victim for the lesson.
explanation: First, check each side of the blank. "Their endings are strikingly uniform" can stand alone. Now look past the opening phrase "collected decades apart from narrators who had never met": it is followed by a subject and verb, "fifty-eight of the versions close," so the second part can stand alone too. Two complete sentences need a period or a semicolon, which leaves A and B. Next, decide which sentence "however" belongs to. The contrast is between the previous sentence (the versions disagree about almost everything) and this one (their endings are uniform), so "however" goes with the first clause. The second clause doesn't contrast with anything. It gives the evidence that the endings are uniform. Choice A places "however" correctly and ends the first sentence after it.

B.why: You were right that two sentences meet here and that a period is needed, but you put "however" on the wrong side of it. Starting the second sentence with "However" sets the 58 matching endings against the claim that the endings are uniform, when they actually prove it. The contrast is with the earlier sentence about the versions disagreeing, so "however" belongs before the period.

C.why: You read "collected decades apart..." as a phrase describing "endings" and assumed a comma was enough. That phrase actually introduces a new main clause, "fifty-eight of the versions close," so a comma alone joins two complete sentences. That is a comma splice, even with "however" set off by commas.

D.why: With no punctuation, two complete sentences run together into a fused sentence. "However" also floats between them, so it isn't clear which clause it belongs to. A long sentence still needs a boundary where one complete thought ends and another begins.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In the early 1970s, Curitiba, Brazil, could not afford the subway its planners wanted. What those planners realized, long before the phrase "bus rapid transit" entered their profession's vocabulary, was that a bus could behave like a train if it never had to wait in traffic or at the curb ______ given its own lanes, raised boarding stations, and fares collected before entry, a bus could move almost as steadily as a subway car.
explanation: Check the left side first. It opens with "What those planners realized," which looks like a fragment, but that whole noun clause is the subject. If you cross out the interrupter about "bus rapid transit," you're left with "What those planners realized was that a bus could behave like a train...", which is a complete sentence. Now the right side: after the opening phrase "given its own lanes, raised boarding stations, and fares collected before entry" comes a subject and verb, "a bus could move," so it is also a complete sentence. Two complete sentences can be joined by a semicolon, and no extra conjunction is needed. Choice C is correct.

A.why: One of two misreadings brings you here. Either you took "What those planners realized..." as a dependent fragment, or you took "given its own lanes..." as a modifier hanging off the first sentence. Neither is true. The subject and verb "a bus could move" make the second part a complete sentence, so a comma alone creates a comma splice.

B.why: This runs two complete sentences together with no punctuation. Because the second one opens with "given," it can look like it is continuing the first. But "a bus could move" starts a new main clause, so the two need a boundary.

D.why: You correctly saw two complete sentences, then joined them twice. A semicolon already does the joining, so adding "and" after it is redundant and nonstandard. Use either a semicolon alone or a comma plus "and," not both.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Folklorist Ines Varga recorded forty-one tellings of a Carpathian tale in which a miller tricks a frost spirit out of a winter's grain. To her surprise, the plot barely shifted across the region: the bargain, the riddle, and the sudden thaw arrived in the same order every time. Varying instead was the spirit's ______ which valley the teller called home.
choices: name; chosen by each teller, it signaled
name, chosen by each teller, it signaled
name; chosen by each teller, signaled
name, chosen by each teller, signaled
explanation: The part before the blank is inverted, but it is still a full sentence: "Varying instead was the spirit's name" means "the spirit's name was varying instead." After the blank, "chosen by each teller" is only an opening modifier, and "it signaled which valley..." is a second full sentence with its own subject and verb. Two full sentences need a semicolon (or a period) between them. Only choice A gives you both the semicolon and the subject "it" that the second sentence needs.

B.why: You read "chosen by each teller" as a modifier describing "name" and stopped there. Keep reading: "it signaled" begins a new full sentence, so this choice joins two full sentences with only a comma. That's a comma splice. You may also have taken the inverted opening clause for a fragment.

C.why: You spotted that a semicolon was needed. But this choice drops "it," so the part after the semicolon ("chosen by each teller, signaled which valley...") has no subject. That makes it a fragment, and a semicolon can't come before a fragment.

D.why: You treated "chosen by each teller" as a pair of commas around an interruption. With that phrase removed, you're left with "Varying instead was the spirit's name signaled which valley...": two main verbs and nothing grammatical joining them.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When the city of Brennick raised its minimum wage by 30 percent, labour economist Teodor Haas expected restaurants to shed workers. But a kitchen needs a fixed number of hands during the dinner rush, and owners could not cut staff without closing ______ trimmed the slow afternoon shifts, leaving headcounts steady while total hours fell.
explanation: "Owners could not cut staff without closing stations" is a full sentence, and so is "they trimmed the slow afternoon shifts." That means the join needs a semicolon. "Instead" says that trimming shifts *replaced* cutting staff, so it belongs at the start of the second clause, with the semicolon in front of it and a comma after it. Choice A does exactly that.

B.why: You treated "instead" as if it could join the two clauses. It can't. It isn't a FANBOYS word, so putting commas around it still leaves two full sentences joined by a comma. That's a comma splice.

C.why: You knew a semicolon was needed but put it on the wrong side of "instead." Now the first clause reads "could not cut staff without closing stations instead," which makes no sense, and the second clause loses the word that marks trimming shifts as the alternative.

D.why: You let "instead" do the joining. A comma followed by a transition adverb still can't hold two full sentences together, so this choice is a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Built to carry rail freight across the Lenne River, the Ridgeway Viaduct still looks massive from the water. Its original piers—poured in 1931 from a concrete mix that, engineers now know, held far too much ______ cracking found by inspectors last spring had started deep inside the piers decades before it reached the surface.
choices: water—were never as sound as they looked; the
water, were never as sound as they looked; the
water—were never as sound as they looked, the
water—never as sound as they looked; the
explanation: This blank has to do three things. (1) The interruption opened with a dash after "piers," so it has to close with a dash. (2) "Its original piers" still needs a main verb, which "were" provides. (3) After that, "the cracking... had started" is a second full sentence, so the join needs a semicolon. Cross out the interruption and you get "Its original piers were never as sound as they looked; the cracking... had started..." Only choice A gets all three right.

B.why: You got the verb and the semicolon right but missed the dash that opened the interruption much earlier, after "piers." Punctuation around an interruption has to match at both ends, so a comma can't close it.

C.why: You closed the interruption correctly, then joined "the piers were never as sound as they looked" to "the cracking... had started..." with only a comma. Both are full sentences, so that's a comma splice. The long interruption is what hides it.

D.why: You got the dash and the semicolon right but lost the verb. Without "were," "Its original piers... never as sound as they looked" has a subject and no main verb. It's a fragment, and a semicolon can't follow a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Health officials in Marvale first tried mailing reminder cards to families whose children were overdue for measles vaccination, and replies stayed below 10 percent ______ nurses began calling parents directly did the clinic's appointment book start to fill. Within two months, the number of overdue children had fallen by half.
explanation: The second clause is inverted: "Only when nurses began calling parents directly did the clinic's appointment book start to fill" means "the book started to fill only when nurses called." That makes it a full sentence with the subject "book" and the verb "did... start." The first part, which already contains its own ", and," is also a full sentence. Two full sentences need a semicolon between them, and "only" has to stay attached to "when," because that pairing is what sets up the inversion. Choice A does both.

B.why: You read "only when..." as a dependent clause, so the second half looked like a fragment that a comma could attach. But "did the clinic's appointment book start" finishes it as a full inverted sentence. Joining it to the first with only a comma makes a comma splice.

C.why: With no punctuation, the two full sentences run straight into each other. That's a fused sentence, and it's easy to miss because "below 10 percent only when" sounds like one phrase.

D.why: You knew a semicolon was needed but put it after "only." That separates "only" from "when," so the right side ("when nurses began calling... did the clinic's appointment book start to fill") is no longer a grammatical sentence. Without "only" at the front, nothing triggers the inverted "did... start."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: For a decade, astronomers at the Kessel Observatory were puzzled by a star that dimmed by 20 percent every 41 days and then recovered. A 2024 study finally proposed an ______ disk of dust orbiting an unseen companion star passes in front of the brighter star on each circuit, blocking part of its light.
explanation: "A 2024 study finally proposed an answer" is a full sentence that points forward to an answer it hasn't given yet. What follows ("a disk of dust... passes in front of the brighter star") is a full sentence that gives that answer. A colon can join two full sentences when the second one explains the first, and that's exactly what happens here. That makes choice A correct.

B.why: You read "a disk of dust orbiting an unseen companion star" as an appositive renaming "answer," and an appositive does take a comma. But the verb "passes" comes later and turns that phrase into the subject of a new full sentence. A comma between two full sentences is a comma splice.

C.why: With no punctuation, "proposed an answer a disk of dust... passes" runs two full sentences together into a fused sentence.

D.why: You saw that two clauses meet here and reached for a semicolon. But adding "that" turns the right side into a noun clause ("that a disk of dust... passes"), which can't stand alone, and a semicolon can't come before a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sailors relied on mapmaker Aurelio Fenn's 1702 chart of the northern strait for decades. It shows the island of Velka as two landmasses divided by a navigable ______ sounding that channel found it barely knee-deep at low tide, and later charts quietly joined the halves.
explanation: "It shows the island of Velka as two landmasses divided by a navigable channel" is a full sentence, and so is "surveyors sounding that channel found it barely knee-deep." They need a semicolon between them. The date and "however" both belong to the second sentence: the surveying happened in 1741, and that finding contradicts the 1702 chart. Both are introductory elements, so each is followed by a comma. Choice A gets all of this right.

B.why: Commas around "in 1741" and "however" make those words look like an interruption, but neither one can join two sentences. In the end, two full sentences are held together by only a comma, which is a comma splice.

C.why: You placed the semicolon correctly but left out the comma after "however." Without it, "however surveyors sounding that channel found..." reads as "in whatever way surveyors found," and the clause stops making grammatical sense.

D.why: This choice puts the semicolon in a grammatically legal spot, but it moves "in 1741" into the first sentence. Now a chart made in 1702 shows a channel "in 1741," which the passage's dates rule out. The date belongs to the surveyors.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In a six-week feeding trial, two groups of adults ate diets matched for calories, protein, and ______ about 90 more calories a day than the group eating refined grains, apparently because more of the whole-grain meals passed through the gut undigested.
choices: fat; eating whole grains rather than refined ones, the first group burned
fat, eating whole grains rather than refined ones, the first group burned
fat; eating whole grains rather than refined ones, the first group burning
fat, eating whole grains rather than refined ones; the first group burned
explanation: "Two groups of adults ate diets matched for calories, protein, and fat" is a full sentence. "Eating whole grains rather than refined ones, the first group burned..." is a second full sentence: it opens with a participle phrase that describes "the first group," and "burned" is its verb. The semicolon has to go between the two sentences, before "eating," so that the phrase describes only the first group. Choice A is the only one that does this.

B.why: The comma after "fat" looks like it continues the list, and "eating whole grains..." looks like a modifier. But "the first group burned" makes everything after "fat" a full sentence, so this choice is a comma splice.

C.why: You placed the semicolon correctly but chose "burning." That's a nonfinite form, so the second half has no main verb and becomes a fragment, which a semicolon can't introduce.

D.why: This choice is punctuated legally, but the semicolon is in the wrong place. "Eating whole grains rather than refined ones" now describes both groups, which contradicts the passage, where only one group ate whole grains and the other ate refined grains.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: At the Tel Sarun excavation, storage jars in the lower granary held charred barley, while those in the upper room, sealed with clay stoppers, held only traces of olive ______ concluded that the two rooms had served different seasons of the farming year.
explanation: The text before the blank is a full sentence; the "while" clause and the phrase "sealed with clay stoppers" are only add-ons to it. "The team concluded..." is a second full sentence. A comma followed by the FANBOYS word "so" is a legal way to join two full sentences, and "so" fits the logic: the different contents led to the conclusion. That makes choice A correct.

B.why: You knew the second clause expressed a result, so you added "therefore." But "therefore" is an adverb, not a conjunction. Putting commas around it doesn't change that two full sentences are joined by only a comma, which is a comma splice.

C.why: You chose the right joining word but put the comma on the wrong side. Between two full sentences the comma goes before "so," not after it, and "so" with no comma in front leaves the sentences fused.

D.why: You treated "therefore" as if it could join clauses the way "so" does. It can't, so this choice is still a comma splice between two full sentences. Swapping in a FANBOYS word or a semicolon would fix it.
